Title: The analysis of generative artificial intelligence technology for innovative thinking and strategies in animation teaching

Xu Yao1, Yaozhang Zhong2 & Weiran Cao3
This work examines the application of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) technology in animation 
teaching, focusing on its role in enhancing teaching quality and learning efficiency through innovative 
instructional strategies. Compared to traditional animation teaching methods, GAI technology 
introduces a novel pedagogical paradigm characterized by adaptive personalized learning pathways, 
intelligent teaching resource optimization, and immersive interactive learning models. A mixed-
methods research approach is adopted, integrating quantitative analysis (experimental data and 
questionnaire surveys) and qualitative analysis (behavioral observations) to systematically assess 
the educational effectiveness of GAI technology. The experiment, conducted over 12 weeks, involved 
120 students divided into an experimental group and a control group. Data sources included pre- 
and post-test evaluations, learning feedback surveys, and classroom behavior analysis. The results 
indicate that, compared to conventional teaching methods, GAI technology significantly enhances 
learning outcomes, knowledge application abilities, learning motivation, and student satisfaction. 
The adaptive personalized learning pathway dynamically adjusts content based on students’ progress, 
improving their mastery of foundational knowledge and skill transferability. Intelligent teaching 
resources automatically generate high-quality animation examples and provide dynamic feedback 
mechanisms, fostering creative expression and practical efficiency. The immersive interactive learning 
model effectively increases classroom engagement, teamwork skills, and problem-solving abilities. 
These findings demonstrate that GAI technology has the potential to transform animation teaching 
by optimizing the learning experience and advancing intelligent teaching methodologies. Beyond 
offering personalized learning solutions, GAI technology plays a crucial role in cultivating students’ 
creativity, critical thinking, and autonomous learning abilities. This work provides theoretical support 
and practical guidance for the digital transformation of animation teaching while underscoring the 
broader applicability of GAI technology in the education sector, offering new directions for the future 
development of intelligent education.

Research background and motivations
In the digital era, the rapid advancement of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) is profoundly transforming 
various fields, including education and entertainment1–3. In the context of animation teaching, GAI technology 
presents unprecedented opportunities and challenges for teaching innovation4–7. This work focuses on animation 
as a technical and creative discipline, rather than as a tool for teaching other subjects. Specifically, it explores 
how GAI facilitates the development of students’ animation skills, creativity, and critical thinking. Traditional 
animation teaching is often constrained by limitations such as manpower, time, and technical resources, making 
it difficult to achieve personalized, flexible, and interactive instruction8,9. The integration of GAI technology 
introduces new possibilities by leveraging intelligent algorithms and big data analysis to establish personalized 
learning pathways, provide real-time feedback, and generate intelligent recommendations. These advancements 
enhance both teaching effectiveness and the overall learning experience10–12.

As a multimedia format, animation offers significant advantages in teaching and learning due to its vivid 
visuals, coherent narratives, and intuitive expression13. However, traditional animation teaching often relies 
on fixed instructional content and methods, limiting its ability to effectively stimulate students’ creativity 
and cognitive development14–16. In recent years, research on GAI has advanced significantly in areas such as 
animation production, style transfer, and intelligent character generation. For instance, studies on automated 
animation generation have demonstrated GAI’s potential to reduce production costs and improve efficiency17. 
Other research has explored how integrating GAI with cognitive science can enhance learner interaction and 
engagement18,19. Additionally, existing literature suggests that deep learning-based GAI technologies can 
diversify animation content and provide technical support for personalized learning20,21.
For example, some scholars have investigated the potential of GAI in artistic creation, proposing that style 
transfer techniques based on Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) can 
enhance students’ understanding of animation aesthetics and foster their creative abilities22. Specifically, GANs 
achieve high-quality content generation through adversarial training between a generator and a discriminator, 
whereas VAEs enhance generative diversity via probabilistic encoding-decoding structures. Furthermore, 
research indicates that utilizing GAI to support autonomous creation significantly increases students’ creative 
interest and accelerates their learning process23. However, despite its vast potential, the practical application 
of GAI in education still faces challenges, such as tailoring learning experiences to individual student needs 
and effectively leveraging intelligent resources for interactive learning. These issues require further in-depth 
exploration and research.
Additionally, several studies have explored the practical applications of GAI in education, emphasizing 
its advantages in personalized instruction and real-time feedback24. For instance, research suggests that 
personalized learning pathways can effectively enhance students’ motivation and strengthen their autonomous 
learning abilities25. However, most existing studies focus on the supplementary role of GAI within traditional 
instructional models, with limited research examining its full integration into animation teaching. In particular, 
there is a lack of studies exploring how personalized learning pathways and intelligent teaching resources can be 
utilized to enhance students’ creative thinking and practical skills.
While GAI technology holds significant potential for animation creation and education, research on its 
effective application in animation instruction remains relatively limited. Current studies primarily examine 
GAI’s role in automated animation production and intelligent content recommendation, with less attention given 
to its impact on fostering students’ creative thinking, collaborative learning, and practical skill development. 
Moreover, a systematic framework for assessing the specific functions and applicability of GAI in animation 
teaching is lacking. Therefore, building upon existing research, this work further investigates the application 
strategies and optimization approaches of GAI in animation teaching to address this research gap and provide 
both theoretical support and practical guidance for future instructional innovation.
Research objectives and contributions
This work is motivated by a critical examination of the limitations of traditional animation teaching methods. 
Existing instructional models struggle to accommodate students’ individualized learning needs, lack efficient 
allocation of intelligent teaching resources, and provide insufficient interactive learning experiences. To address 
these challenges, this work establishes its research objectives and key research questions through an extensive 
review of the literature and a preliminary survey of educators and students in animation teaching.
The primary objective of this work is to investigate how GAI can facilitate personalized learning pathways 
to support diverse student groups. Specifically, it examines how GAI can provide customized learning support 
based on students’ age, learning preferences, and creative proficiency, while also evaluating its impact on learning 
effectiveness and adaptability. Accordingly, this work seeks to answer a central research question: How can GAI-
driven personalized learning pathways effectively address the needs of different student groups and enhance 
animation teaching?
Furthermore, this work evaluates the applicability and effectiveness of intelligent teaching resources across 
various animation tasks and creative themes. While existing research has demonstrated that intelligent resources 
can enhance teaching efficiency, their adaptability across different creative tasks remains insufficiently validated. 
This work employs experimental comparative analysis to examine the use of intelligent teaching resources in 
multiple creative tasks, aiming to identify their universality and limitations. Therefore, the second research 
question is: To what extent do intelligent teaching resources produce consistent effects across different types 
of animation creation tasks and themes, and how do they contribute to stimulating students’ creativity and 
expressive abilities?
Additionally, this work investigates the role of interactive learning experiences in promoting teamwork 
and problem-solving abilities. Animation production often involves collaborative work; however, traditional 
teaching methods still fall short in developing students’ collaboration skills. This work analyzes the impact 
of GAI technology in interactive teaching environments and explores how it optimizes the development of 
teamwork and critical thinking skills. Accordingly, the third research question is: How do interactive learning 
experiences foster teamwork and problem-solving skills in various collaborative scenarios?
This work addresses three key gaps in the current research on the application of GAI in animation teaching. 
First, existing studies have paid limited attention to how GAI can support the personalized learning needs 
of diverse student groups. This work develops a GAI-driven personalized teaching framework that provides 
adaptable learning pathways for students at varying proficiency levels. Second, the adaptability of intelligent 
teaching resources across different animation creation tasks has not been systematically evaluated. This work 
experimentally analyzes the applicability of intelligent resources in various creative contexts, offering data-
driven insights for optimizing teaching resource allocation. Lastly, research on the role of GAI in interactive 
learning environments is still limited. This work explores how GAI can enhance students’ teamwork and

Literature review
In animation education, the application of GAI entails not only a transformation in technical tools but also a 
profound integration with cognitive learning mechanisms. To further elucidate the optimization logic of GAI 
in the learning process, this work adopts Cognitive Load Theory as its theoretical framework. The Cognitive 
Load Theory posits that learners’ cognitive resource allocation is influenced by three types of cognitive load: 
intrinsic cognitive load, determined by the inherent complexity of the task; extraneous cognitive load, caused 
by ineffective presentation of information; and germane cognitive load, which refers to the deliberate cognitive 
effort invested in constructing a coherent knowledge structure. Based on this framework, GAI technologies 
can enhance the balance of cognitive load through several pathways. First, personalized learning path design 
powered by GAI significantly reduces extraneous cognitive load. In traditional animation instruction, students 
frequently experience information redundancy or cognitive overload due to standardized teaching progress 
and fixed task difficulty. For instance, novice learners may become distracted by the procedural complexity of 
keyframe animation, while more advanced students may feel disengaged due to repetitive practice. GAI addresses 
this challenge by analyzing real-time student performance data—such as task completion time and error types—
and dynamically adjusting the difficulty gradient and informational density of the instructional content. For 
example, when the system identifies a student’s insufficient grasp of the “squash and stretch” animation principle, 
it can automatically provide a simplified breakdown video and minimize non-essential operational cues, thereby 
preventing information overload. This dynamic adaptation mechanism enables precise alignment between 
instructional resources and a learner’s current capabilities, reducing the additional cognitive burden caused 
by inadequate instructional design. Furthermore, the real-time feedback mechanism offered by GAI effectively 
alleviates intrinsic cognitive load. Animation production requires the integration of multiple skill dimensions, 
including narrative logic, visual expression, and software operation. In traditional instructional settings, it is 
often difficult for instructors to address each student’s individual learning challenges in a timely manner. For 
example, a student may produce rigid character movements due to a misunderstanding of physical motion 
principles, yet struggle to identify the root cause of the issue. GAI can address such problems through intelligent 
diagnostic tools—such as motion smoothness analysis algorithms—that promptly detect critical deficiencies 
in student work and generate targeted feedback (e.g., “Adjust the transition curves between frames 5 and 8 to 
enhance natural motion”). This real-time corrective mechanism enables learners to focus cognitive resources 
on internalizing core concepts rather than expending effort on repeated trial-and-error corrections. Moreover, 
GAI’s capability to generate multimodal instructional resources enhances germane cognitive load. Germane 
load reflects the learner’s active cognitive investment in constructing knowledge structures, which is often 
stimulated by interest-driven and context-rich task design. For instance, in a “fantasy scene design” assignment, 
GAI can automatically generate a tailored reference library—including color schemes and architectural element 
sketches—based on students’ preferred artistic styles (such as cyberpunk or ink-wash painting), along with 
embedded narrative prompts (e.g., “How can lighting contrast be used to heighten the sense of mystery in the 
scene?”). This type of personalized, contextualized design not only boosts learning motivation but also channels 
cognitive resources toward creative expression and knowledge transfer, rather than mechanical execution of 
standardized procedures. In addition, GAI-generated virtual mentors can simulate creative dialogues through 
natural language interactions. For example, by asking questions such as “If a character is running in the rain, how 
can motion design convey a sense of emotional tension?”, these systems guide learners to engage in reflective 
application of animation principles.
The application of GAI technology in education, particularly in innovative animation teaching, has 
increasingly garnered attention from researchers, leading to a series of relevant studies. First, some studies 
have focused on specific applications of GAI technology in animation teaching. For instance, research has 
demonstrated favorable teaching outcomes using GAI to generate character design concepts tailored to students’ 
preferences26. Moreover, other studies have explored the impact of GAI technology on animation teaching 
models and methods. For example, a study investigated a GAI-based personalized animation teaching model, 
where students’ learning data and behaviors were analyzed using intelligent algorithms and machine learning 
techniques. This approach provided personalized learning paths and feedback, resulting in a more customized 
animation teaching experience27. Additionally, some research has focused on the innovation of animation 
teaching resources and tools through GAI technology. For example, scholars have proposed a GAI-based 
animation production tool that integrates intelligent algorithms with big data analysis. This tool autonomously 
generates animation scenes and character actions, offering both teachers and students a more convenient and 
efficient animation production platform28. These studies provide new possibilities for the development and 
utilization of animation teaching resources, advancing the intelligent and personalized evolution of animation 
teaching tools.
Over the years, the application of GAI in education has garnered significant attention and research. The 
following insights from relevant scholars highlight key findings in this area. One study emphasized the 
effectiveness of GAI technology in designing personalized learning paths. By adjusting the difficulty and style of 
teaching content based on students’ learning abilities and interests, GAI better meets their needs and enhances 
their engagement levels29. This personalized approach not only improves learning outcomes but also boosts 
students’ interest and motivation. Another study explored the application of GAI in education, focusing on the 
importance of real-time monitoring of student progress and feedback30. The researchers found that GAI could 
assist teachers in adjusting instructional strategies promptly, facilitating more flexible and effective teaching 
methods—critical for improving teaching quality. Additionally, scholars have studied the development and

Other studies have proposed that the real-time monitoring capabilities of GAI technology can help teachers

accordingly33. This flexibility enhances the effectiveness of teaching paths in meeting personalized learning 
needs. Additionally, some scholars researched the development of intelligent teaching resources and found that 
GAI animation tools improved students’ efficiency in creating animations, while also stimulating their creativity 
and expressive abilities34. These resources could also offer personalized learning advice, aiding students 
in better grasping knowledge and skills. Furthermore, researchers pointed out that personalized learning 
recommendations and assistance provided by intelligent teaching resources can significantly enhance students’ 
learning outcomes35. This GAI-based approach to resource development offers targeted learning support by 
utilizing students’ learning data and behaviors. Other scholars investigated the construction of interactive 
learning experiences and suggested that through virtual laboratories and interactions with virtual characters, 
students could practice operations in a virtual environment while receiving real-time feedback. This approach 
deepens their understanding of animation creation principles and techniques36.
For example, one study designed an application called Build_PC, which allows students to visualize and 
assemble hardware components in a virtual environment overlaid onto the real world. This enables hands-
on learning of computer assembly37. Other studies hosted workshops on creative creation using text-to-
image generative AI to stimulate discussions about generative AI and explore imaginative concepts38. The 
results indicated that incorporating AI into creative projects prompted instructors to reflect on the unique 
nature of craftsmanship, as well as the tensions and trade-offs involved in adopting generative AI in practical 
craftwork. Additionally, scholars developed a model for integrating technical teaching content and conducted a 
comprehensive evaluation of various studies to explore animation design courses in design education, student 
perception preferences, and difficulty levels. This facilitated research and analysis of AI technology in the 
context of animation design39. In a comparative experimental study with 40 first-year students majoring in 
animation design, the results showed that combining online design studio projects with personalized project 
learning guidance led to improved trends in students’ learning needs. Customized learning and project practice 
content enhanced both the learning experience and performance of the students. Furthermore, literature 
comparing two groups of students from different academic backgrounds who underwent the same experimental 
conditions and used various AI platforms to design, develop, and implement instructional design projects to 
create multimedia content for their respective disciplines revealed interesting findings40. The results showed 
that both groups achieved similar learning outcomes in project design, development, and implementation. In 
terms of user experience, both groups reported similar overall outcomes. However, students majoring in early 
childhood education rated the usefulness of AI multimedia platforms much higher, while computer science 
students reported slightly higher comfort levels with these tools.
In conclusion, current research has made significant progress in the application of GAI technology in 
education, particularly in animation teaching. Existing studies primarily focus on the following key aspects: 
First, specific case studies of GAI applications in animation teaching, such as the use of GAI technology to 
generate character design solutions tailored to students’ preferences, which have resulted in favorable teaching 
outcomes. Second, the impact of GAI technology on animation teaching models and methods, including 
personalized animation teaching models based on GAI that provide customized learning paths and feedback 
by analyzing students’ learning data and behavior. Third, the application of GAI in the innovation of animation 
teaching resources and tools, such as GAI-based animation production tools that automatically generate 
animation scenes and character movements, providing a more convenient production platform for both teachers 
and students. Additionally, scholars have explored the potential of GAI technology in areas such as personalized 
learning path design, real-time monitoring of learning progress, intelligent teaching resource development, 
and the creation of interactive learning experiences. GAI technology also facilitates intelligent dialogues and 
behaviors with virtual characters, promoting personalized interactions with students to enhance their learning 
interests and enthusiasm. Integrating the insights from these studies offers a comprehensive understanding of 
the application of GAI in animation teaching, providing a solid theoretical foundation and practical guidance 
for future advancements in this field.
Based on the theoretical perspectives outlined above, this work proposes the following original hypotheses:
	1.	 Personalized learning paths significantly enhance students’ mastery of fundamental knowledge and their 
ability to apply it effectively.
	2.	 Intelligent teaching resources substantially improve the quality and efficiency of students’ creative work.
	3.	 Interactive learning experiences notably increase student engagement, teamwork abilities, and problem-solv­
ing skills.
In summary, while existing research provides valuable insights into the application of GAI technology in 
animation teaching, several research gaps remain. First, current studies tend to focus on individual technological 
applications or teaching models, with limited exploration of the systematic integration of GAI technology within 
the broader animation teaching framework. Second, research on how GAI technology specifically enhances 
students’ creativity, cognitive abilities, and learning motivation remains scarce, particularly due to the lack of 
long-term experimental data. Additionally, there is a noticeable gap in studies evaluating the actual teaching

Research methodology
Animation teaching models and methods based on GAI
In a GAI environment, innovating animation teaching models and methods plays a crucial role in enhancing 
both teaching quality and learning efficiency41. Table 1 outlines the implementation strategies and anticipated 
effects of animation teaching models and methods within the GAI context:
Personalized teaching path design allows for the adjustment of teaching content’s difficulty and style according 
to students’ learning abilities and interests, thereby tailoring it to their specific needs and acceptance levels. 
Moreover, the integration of GAI technology facilitates real-time monitoring of students’ learning progress 
and feedback, enabling timely adjustments to instructional strategies. This ensures a more flexible and effective 
teaching path. The development of intelligent teaching resources, such as GAI-based animation production tools, 
empowers students to quickly create personalized animation works, stimulating their creativity and expressive 
abilities. Additionally, these intelligent resources can offer personalized learning suggestions and support based 
on students’ learning data and behaviors, helping them better grasp knowledge and refine skills.
Interactive learning experience construction involves virtual laboratories and interactions with virtual 
characters, allowing students to engage in hands-on operations and receive real-time feedback within a virtual 
environment. This process deepens their understanding of animation production principles and techniques. 
Furthermore, leveraging GAI technology enables intelligent dialogue and behaviors of virtual characters, 
fostering personalized interactions that spark students’ interest and enthusiasm for learning. By enhancing 
students’ learning outcomes, these interactive experiences also cultivate teamwork and problem-solving abilities, 
promoting holistic development in animation teaching.
Innovative thinking and strategies applied to animation teaching
In this context, innovative thinking refers to the generation of new ideas and problem-solving approaches 
through creativity, which stimulates students’ innovative potential and is crucial for animation teaching. 
Innovative strategies, on the other hand, involve the application of novel teaching methods and tools, 
particularly GAI technology, to enhance teaching effectiveness and promote active learning. The theoretical 
foundation of this work integrates research on creativity, educational innovation, and the latest advancements 
in AI technology. Specifically, this work defines “innovative strategies” in animation teaching across three key 
dimensions: personalized teaching paths, intelligent teaching resource development, and interactive learning 
environments. Personalized teaching paths involve creating tailored learning trajectories based on students’ 
real-time performance and preferences. Intelligent teaching resource development leverages GAI tools to create 
dynamic and adaptive teaching materials that respond to student needs. Interactive learning environments foster 
student engagement and teamwork by designing collaborative problem-solving activities, guided by AI-driven 
facilitation.
In the context of animation teaching within a GAI environment, establishing mechanisms to foster student 
engagement and collaboration is essential52. Introducing cooperative learning and project-based learning can 
stimulate students’ teamwork awareness and creativity53. For example, students can be organized into groups 
to complete an animation production project, with each group responsible for specific tasks, such as character 
design, scene creation, and animation production. Throughout the process, students collaborate, exchange ideas, 
and solve problems, which enhances teamwork and communication skills. Furthermore, GAI technology can 
provide real-time collaboration platforms and tools, enabling students to engage in remote collaboration and 
joint editing, thereby improving participation and cooperation efficiency54–56.

Inspiration stimulation and expression cultivation are key strategies for fostering innovation in animation 
teaching within a GAI environment57. By designing challenging and inspirational tasks, students can be guided 
to develop their creative thinking and expressive abilities58. For instance, providing open-ended animation 
themes or scene settings encourages students to unleash their imagination and creativity, allowing them to 
freely express personal perspectives and emotions. Additionally, intelligent algorithms and creative generation 
tools powered by GAI technology can offer students creative inspiration and technical support, helping them 
overcome creative challenges and achieve expressive outcomes. Teachers can further promote peer learning 
and communication through regular creative sharing and evaluation activities, collectively enhancing students’ 
creative skills and expressive capabilities59–62.
In GAI-based animation teaching, both the roles of teachers and the associated teaching management 
strategies require optimization and adjustment63,64. Teachers are no longer merely knowledge transmitters; they 
serve as guides, facilitators, and promoters of student learning. It is crucial for teachers to address students’ 
individualized needs and monitor their learning progress, adapting teaching content and methods to provide 
personalized support. Moreover, teachers should actively engage in students’ learning activities, fostering 
open discussions to resolve challenges and collaboratively solve problems. This approach not only helps to 
overcome learning obstacles but also strengthens the teacher-student relationship, fostering a positive learning 
environment. Furthermore, by utilizing data analysis and feedback tools powered by GAI technology, teachers 
can obtain real-time insights into students’ progress and offer immediate, tailored support. This enables teachers 
to adjust instructional strategies and management practices accordingly, promoting smoother teaching processes 
and improved learning outcomes65–68. In summary, Fig. 1 illustrates the application structure framework of 
innovative thinking and strategies in animation teaching.
To create a personalized, flexible, and engaging learning experience, this work employs an interactive learning 
platform powered by GAI. Specifically designed for animation teaching, the platform enhances creativity, 
collaboration, and critical thinking. Utilizing GAI algorithms, it develops personalized learning paths tailored 
to each student’s progress, interests, and skill levels. These learning paths are dynamically adjusted based on 
continuous feedback and data analysis, ensuring that each student receives an optimal learning plan. Throughout 
the creative process, students benefit from immediate real-time feedback and AI-generated suggestions for 
improvement, enabling them to refine and enhance their creative outcomes. Additionally, the platform provides 
collaborative tools that facilitate team-based learning, allowing students to edit projects in real-time and share 
ideas through discussion boards. Interactive dashboards displaying the team’s overall progress further boost 
collaboration and interactivity.
To illustrate the platform’s practical application, consider a student group working on an animation project. 
A high school student with limited drawing skills used the platform’s AI-assisted features to transform sketches 
into professional-quality animation materials, which significantly increased their confidence and creativity. 
Meanwhile, a team of three college students collaborated on a short animated film, leveraging the platform’s real-
time collaboration tools to manage work progress, exchange ideas, and resolve issues related to plot coherence 
and visual consistency with AI-generated insights. The platform also integrates gamification elements—such as 
achievement badges and progress milestones—motivating students to explore new technologies and complete 
tasks efficiently, thereby further enhancing student engagement and motivation.

of measurement indicators that integrate both quantitative and qualitative methods. These indicators cover three 
key dimensions: creativity enhancement, teaching effectiveness, and engagement and interaction. For creativity

Additionally, within the mixed-methods design of this work, we strengthened the analysis of qualitative 
data to gain deeper insights into students’ animation learning experiences facilitated by GAI. Specifically, we 
conducted semi-structured interviews and administered open-ended questionnaires, followed by thematic 
analysis, to identify the core learning experiences and challenges faced by students in the GAI-supported 
teaching environment. The interview questions focused on the role of GAI in personalized learning paths, 
creativity enhancement, and teamwork collaboration. Data analysis was performed using coding software, which 
allowed us to identify key themes, including “effectiveness of automated feedback,” “perceptions of creativity 
enhancement,” and “technical barriers and adaptability.”
Experimental design and performance evaluation
Research design and dataset collection
This work employs a mixed-methods research approach, integrating both quantitative and qualitative methods 
to thoroughly evaluate the effectiveness of GAI in animation teaching. The rationale behind this approach is to 
capture both measurable outcomes (quantitative data) and deeper contextual insights (qualitative data) from 
students’ learning experiences. This combination enables a more comprehensive understanding of how GAI-
driven innovative thinking and strategies enhance the effectiveness of animation teaching. For the quantitative 
aspect, pre- and post-tests are utilized to assess students’ performance in basic knowledge and application ability. 
Additionally, structured questionnaires are administered to measure students’ learning satisfaction, motivation, 
and engagement. Statistical methods such as t-tests, analysis of variance (ANOVA), and effect size calculations 
are used to compare differences in knowledge retention, application ability, and other learning outcomes 
between the experimental and control groups. Regarding qualitative methods, data is collected through 
student interviews, open-ended questionnaires, and classroom observations. These methods aim to provide 
an in-depth understanding of students’ learning experiences and explore the impact of personalized learning 
paths, intelligent teaching resources, and AI-enabled interactive learning environments. The qualitative data is 
analyzed using thematic analysis to identify and discuss key themes related to learning engagement, creativity, 
problem-solving skills, and teamwork.

To enhance the transparency of the experimental design and ensure the validity and credibility of the results, 
a strict random grouping method is employed for the control and experimental groups. A series of statistical 
tests are conducted to verify that there are no significant differences in students’ baseline characteristics prior 
to the experiment, thus eliminating potential bias. First, simple random sampling is used to assign students 
to the control and experimental groups. This process involves randomly selecting participants from the total 
pool, ensuring each student has an equal chance of being placed in either group. This approach mitigates any 
human bias in the grouping process, ensuring fairness and scientific rigor. To confirm that the two groups are 
comparable before the experiment, statistical tests are applied. Chi-square tests are used to compare gender 
distribution between the groups, while independent samples t-tests are employed to assess other background 
variables, such as age and academic performance. The results reveal no significant differences between the 
control and experimental groups in terms of age, gender, or academic performance (p > 0.05). This indicates that 
the groups are comparable at the start of the experiment, ensuring the reliability of the findings.
To assess the impact of personalized teaching paths, intelligent teaching resources, and interactive learning 
experiences on student learning outcomes, various experimental scenarios are designed based on the study’s 
objectives and hypotheses. These scenarios include animation production tasks and interactive learning activities 
of varying levels of difficulty. Specifically, three levels of difficulty are established for the animation production 
tasks (basic, intermediate, and advanced), along with three types of interactive learning tasks (individual tasks, 
group discussions, and collective creation). These scenarios are intended to comprehensively evaluate students’ 
animation creation capabilities and collaborative skills. Prior to the formal experiment, a pilot test is conducted 
for all experimental tasks to ensure that tasks of varying difficulty are appropriately challenging for both groups 
and can effectively distinguish differences in learning progress. During the pilot test, completion time, task 
difficulty, and student feedback for each task are assessed. Tasks deemed too simple or too complex are then 
adjusted accordingly. The results of the pilot test confirm that the difficulty distribution of all tasks is well-
balanced between the control and experimental groups, ensuring the fairness and reliability of the experiment.
Experimental environment and parameters setting
This work explores innovative thinking and strategies in animation teaching within a GAI environment. A 
comprehensive experimental environment is established, including hardware, software, and experimental 
conditions tailored to the study’s needs. The experimental computer is a high-performance workstation featuring 
an NVIDIA RTX 3090 graphics card and an Intel i9-10900 K processor, supported by 64GB of memory and a 
1 TB SSD. This configuration enables large-scale data processing and deep learning model training, providing the 
necessary computational power for the study. A development environment based on the Python programming 
language is set up, utilizing popular deep learning frameworks such as TensorFlow and PyTorch. These 
frameworks offer a wide range of GAI algorithm implementations, including GAN and VAE, ensuring robust 
technical support for the research. For dataset selection, the Disney Movies and Films Dataset, an open-source 
dataset, is employed. This dataset provides a diverse foundation for the experiments. In terms of experimental 
conditions, various scenarios are designed in alignment with the research objectives and requirements. Factors 
such as students’ age, gender, and learning preferences are considered when developing different teaching tasks 
and learning scenarios. The experimental tasks include animation production assignments of varying difficulty 
levels, as well as diverse animation material presentations and interactive learning experiences. These setups aim 
to explore the teaching effectiveness and learning outcomes across multiple conditions.
Statistical analysis method
To ensure the robustness and validity of the research findings, this work employs a more refined and systematic 
data analysis approach, combining both descriptive and inferential statistical analyses. In the descriptive 
statistical analysis, all data are comprehensively organized and summarized, focusing on the central tendencies 
and dispersion of the pre- and post-test scores, survey results, and behavioral data for both the experimental and 
control groups. Specifically, key statistical measures, including means, standard deviations, weighted means, and 
interquartile ranges for each group, are calculated, which helps in understanding the overall performance trends 
and variations of students during the experimental process. Additionally, to ensure comprehensive visualization 
of the data, SPSS software (version 26.0) is used to generate frequency distributions, histograms, and box plots, 
providing a more intuitive presentation of the data distribution, including skewness, kurtosis, and potential 
outliers within each group’s score distribution. This process assists in the preliminary identification of any 
anomalies or extreme values in the data, offering a foundation for further in-depth analysis.
In the inferential statistical analysis section, this work employs two methods: independent samples t-test 
and One-Way ANOVA to examine significant differences between the experimental groups. The independent 
samples t-test is used to compare mean differences between the experimental and control groups, testing 
whether differences in student performance, motivational changes, satisfaction, and other factors are statistically 
significant. To ensure the accuracy of the t-test, a normality test is performed on the data before analysis, using 
the Shapiro-Wilk test to determine whether the data follow a normal distribution. If the p-value exceeds 0.05, 
the data are considered to follow a normal distribution; if the p-value is less than 0.05, it suggests that the data 
may not follow a normal distribution, necessitating the use of non-parametric tests (such as the Mann-Whitney 
U test) as alternatives. Furthermore, Levene’s test is conducted to assess the homogeneity of variance between

Evaluation of the effectiveness of personalized teaching path design
A series of performance evaluation indicators and experiments are designed to comprehensively assess the 
effectiveness of innovative thinking and strategies in animation teaching within a GAI environment. The 
experiment involves two groups: the control group, which follows a traditional uniform teaching path, and the 
experimental group, which follows a personalized teaching path customized using GAI technology. Spanning 
12 weeks, the experiment includes four teaching activities per week, each lasting 2 h. A basic knowledge test 
is administered to assess students’ understanding of foundational concepts in animation production. This 
test is crucial for determining whether personalized learning paths tailored by GAI contribute to a deeper 
understanding of the essential knowledge and skills required for animation. The content of the test focuses on 
fundamental animation concepts, including principles of animation (e.g., timing, spacing, and squash/stretch 
techniques), narrative foundations (e.g., story structure and character development), and basic technical skills 
(e.g., the use of software tools and visual composition). The goal of the test is to evaluate students’ retention 
and application abilities regarding core animation knowledge, which is essential for producing high-quality 
animated works. The objective is to assess whether personalized teaching paths enabled by AI can enhance 
students’ understanding of these core principles and whether they are more effective than traditional, one-size-
fits-all teaching methods. This aligns with the broader aim of exploring how AI-driven personalized teaching can 
improve students’ retention and application of foundational knowledge in animation production. The impact of 
innovative instructional strategies on students’ mastery of fundamental animation concepts can be evaluated by 
comparing the test results of the experimental group (using personalized AI-driven teaching) with the control 
group (using conventional teaching methods). The test format includes a mix of multiple-choice questions, 
short-answer questions, and practical problem-solving tasks, assessing both theoretical understanding and 
practical application abilities. Each student’s score, ranging from 0 to 100, can be used to compare knowledge 
retention levels between the two groups. The main evaluation indicators include students’ learning outcomes,

Discussion
Current research on GAI in animation education has largely concentrated on tool development or the 
implementation of specific technologies. For instance, GANs have been employed to automate character 
design, while VAEs have been used for style transfer. However, such studies are often limited to demonstrating 
technical capabilities, lacking systematic integration into pedagogical strategies and failing to fully consider the 
synergistic effects of dynamic learning needs and multimodal interaction. The present work addresses these gaps 
through three key innovations. First, a real-time optimization mechanism for dynamically personalized learning 
pathways has been proposed. Existing research predominantly relies on static learning recommendation models, 
such as fixed path planning based on initial skill assessments, which are insufficient for capturing the nonlinear 
and iterative nature of learning in animation creation. For example, the animation teaching system developed by 
Cevahir et al. (2022) allocates tasks based solely on pre-test scores, thereby lacking responsiveness to real-time 
performance differences during collaborative projects69. In this work, a dynamic path optimization algorithm 
based on reinforcement learning was constructed by integrating multi-source data—including operational logs, 
iterative versions of creative work, and peer review feedback. This algorithm adjusts task complexity according 
to individual progress and identifies complementary needs within team collaboration. For instance, during 
the storyboard writing phase, students with weaker narrative skills are automatically assigned supplementary 
exercises in visual composition, while those with strong technical skills receive advanced training in rendering 
techniques. This dual-dimension adaptation mechanism—addressing both individual and group needs—
significantly enhances the pedagogical flexibility of complex animation projects. Second, a multi-task-oriented 
intelligent teaching resource library has been developed. Existing GAI-based animation teaching tools are 
often developed for single-task scenarios—such as character generation or scene rendering—which results in 
challenges related to tool switching and knowledge fragmentation during cross-task creative processes. For 
example, although the animation generation tool developed by Kang et al. (2024) supports character motion 
design70, it lacks integration with screenplay development and sound synthesis. To address this issue, the present 
work introduces a modular resource library architecture that leverages a unified knowledge graph to integrate 
animation principles, technical tools, and creative cases. For instance, in a “sci-fi animation short film” project, 
the system can automatically connect character design (via GANs), physical simulation (using rigid body 
dynamics engines), and narrative logic (through natural language processing models), thereby generating cross-
module creative suggestions. This seamless integration of multimodal resources enables students to focus on 
creative expression rather than technical minutiae, overcoming the functional silos typical of traditional tools. 
Third, a collaborative mixed-reality interactive environment has been developed. Existing virtual laboratories 
often rely on unidirectional operation simulations—such as VR-based animation workflow training—and lack 
the social presence and real-time co-creation support required for authentic team collaboration. For example, 
the VR animation platform developed by Li et al. (2023) only supports individual operation71, failing to facilitate 
multi-user real-time editing and AI-assisted guidance. In response, this work combines AR with a distributed 
GAI engine to construct a mixed-reality collaborative space. During group animation projects, students can use 
AR glasses to overlay virtual storyboard sketches on a physical table, which are then synchronized in real time 
to a cloud platform. The GAI assistant, based on multi-user operation data—such as drawing strokes and voice 
discussion keywords—automatically generates conflict-resolution suggestions. This “human-AI-environment”

The findings indicate that AI-based teaching methods significantly enhance student engagement, creativity, 
and problem-solving abilities. Students report that AI tools allow them to learn at their own pace and receive 
immediate feedback, fostering greater motivation and engagement—both crucial factors for successful learning 
outcomes. AI tools provide new avenues for students to express their ideas and explore creativity. In a personalized 
learning environment, students can experiment with different animation techniques, take creative risks, and 
achieve higher-quality results in their projects. These results suggest that AI is a valuable tool in animation 
teaching, particularly in promoting personalized learning and interactive teaching. Teachers can leverage AI to 
provide real-time feedback, tailor learning experiences to individual student needs, and design collaborative, 
problem-solving-oriented activities. Future research can explore how AI fosters creativity and engagement 
in other disciplines and how it can be effectively implemented in larger classroom settings. Moreover, these 
positive outcomes align with existing literature, further reinforcing the potential and value of GAI technology 
in education.
First, previous research has analyzed students’ preferences and responses to different styles of animated 
characters. Researchers successfully employed GAI technology to generate character design schemes tailored 
to students’ preferences, achieving positive teaching outcomes72. These findings align with the results presented 
here, indicating that personalized teaching path design effectively enhances students’ learning experiences and 
outcomes. Additionally, other studies have used intelligent algorithms and machine learning techniques to 
provide personalized learning paths and feedback, enabling customized animation teaching73. This work further 
extends these insights by demonstrating the practical effectiveness of personalized teaching path design through 
empirical research. It highlights the significant role of intelligent teaching resources in improving students’ 
creative quality and efficiency.
Through the development of intelligent teaching resources, students gain a deeper understanding and 
mastery of animation production principles and techniques, enhancing their creativity and expressive abilities. 
Furthermore, this work suggests that constructing interactive learning experiences effectively strengthens 
students’ teamwork and problem-solving abilities. This finding is consistent with existing literature on the 
application of VR and AR technologies in education. For example, some scholars have pointed out that immersive 
learning environments created through VR technology promote active participation and collaborative learning 
among students, thereby improving learning outcomes74. In conclusion, these findings support and expand 
upon previous research, collectively advancing the application and development of GAI in animation teaching.
However, this work relies on a high-performance computing environment and advanced deep learning 
frameworks, such as TensorFlow and PyTorch, for training and deploying GAI models. In practical educational 
settings, particularly in resource-constrained institutions or schools in developing countries, the high 
computational costs and hardware requirements may present significant challenges to the widespread adoption 
of GAI in animation teaching. Therefore, exploring the applicability of GAI-based instructional methods in low-
tech environments is crucial for enhancing their scalability and broader implementation.
For schools with limited computational resources, cloud-based AI solutions can offer a viable alternative. 
In this model, teachers and students can remotely access pre-trained GAI models via cloud-based Application 
Programming Interfaces (APIs) (such as Google Cloud AI, RunwayML, or OpenAI API), eliminating the need 
for locally deploying complex deep learning frameworks. This approach significantly reduces computational 
resource demands while providing flexible instructional support. For example, in some experiments, we utilized 
RunwayML for cloud-based animation generation tests, achieving good performance in tasks such as image 
stylization, automatic keyframe generation, and character animation. Moreover, it can run via APIs on standard 
PCs or even low-spec devices like iPads or Chromebooks. However, despite the feasibility of cloud computing, 
its reliance on a stable internet connection presents challenges for regions with poor network infrastructure. 
Therefore, future research will focus on developing offline versions of lightweight GAI tools. This can be achieved 
by optimizing the size of GAI models through techniques like model quantization and knowledge distillation, 
enabling them to run on local computing devices.
Conclusion
Research contribution
This work makes several significant contributions to the application of GAI in animation teaching. First, 
it empirically validates the effectiveness of GAI technology in personalized teaching path design, intelligent 
teaching resource development, and the creation of interactive learning experiences. These findings not only 
offer new perspectives and methods for animation teaching but also provide valuable insights for educational 
innovation in other disciplines. Second, this work highlights the potential of intelligent teaching resources to 
stimulate students’ creativity and expression. By leveraging GAI-based animation production tools, students can 
create personalized animation projects more efficiently, enhancing both the richness of teaching resources and 
the appeal and practicality of the curriculum. Finally, the research underscores the importance of interactive 
learning experiences in improving students’ teamwork and problem-solving abilities. This aspect plays a crucial 
role in fostering students’ overall skills and adaptability, preparing them for the challenges of future society.
To support educators in applying the findings of this work to practical teaching, several strategies can be 
employed based on learners’ levels in animation design. For beginners, GAI can analyze student behavior (e.g., 
the time spent and frequency of watching teaching videos) and assess their knowledge mastery. Based on this 
data, GAI can automatically generate reinforcement paths to strengthen basic knowledge. For more advanced 
learners, project-oriented learning paths can be developed, such as using GANs to generate complex animation 
scene materials, encouraging independent creation and optimization.nThe development of a GAI-based material 
library can further enhance teaching. Teachers can offer creative references or practice content to students, such

Future works and research limitations
Although this work has validated the effectiveness of Generative GAI in animation education, its technological 
implementation still relies on high-performance computing devices and complex deep learning frameworks 
(e.g., TensorFlow, PyTorch), which limits its application in resource-constrained environments (such as schools 
in developing countries or low-bandwidth regions). To overcome this limitation, future research could focus on 
optimizing the following technical approaches:
For low-configured devices, a model compression solution based on Knowledge Distillation is proposed. 
For instance, pre-trained GANs could be employed through a teacher-student model architecture, transferring 
the knowledge of a complex teacher model to a lightweight student model. This would reduce the model’s 
computational load while ensuring the quality of generation. Additionally, by incorporating Model Quantization 
technology, the model could run on edge devices such as Jetson Nano. Moreover, exploring edge-side inference 
optimization based on the Apple Neural Engine could enable localized GAI animation generation through 
hardware acceleration, thereby reducing reliance on cloud services.
For regions with unstable network connections, a layered caching and incremental update mechanism 
is proposed. For instance, lightweight foundational models (such as keyframe generation modules) could 
be preloaded on local devices, while high-precision models (such as physics simulation engines) would be 
dynamically called via cloud APIs (e.g., Google Cloud AI or RunwayML). In the event of a network interruption, 
the system could automatically switch to the local model to maintain basic functionality, and once the network 
is restored, incremental parameter updates would be synchronized.
In mathematics education, a GAI-based dynamic geometry teaching module is designed. For example, 
Conditional GANs could be used to generate real-time animations of function graphs as parameters change, 
incorporating interactive questioning. In physics education, a GAI simulator based on a physics engine could 
be developed to transform electromagnetic field equations into visual particle motion animations, supporting 
students in adjusting field strength parameters through gesture interaction. The key technical challenges to 
address for these applications include cross-modal data alignment, real-time rendering efficiency optimization, 
and error boundary control.
A sign language animation generation tool is being developed for special education groups, such as students 
with hearing impairments. This tool combines pose estimation models (e.g., OpenPose) with natural language 
processing to convert the teacher’s spoken explanations into real-time sign language animations performed by 
a virtual character, along with automatically generated subtitles. This functionality must address the challenge 
of multimodal temporal synchronization, such as accurately matching gesture movements with the rhythm of 
speech, and design a low-latency transmission protocol to ensure smooth real-time interaction.
The implementation of these technical solutions must consider the unique characteristics of educational 
settings. For instance, during the model lightweighting process, a balance must be struck between generation 
quality and computational cost—excessive compression may result in a loss of animation detail, while high-
fidelity requirements may exceed device computational capacity. To address this, adaptive quality adjustment 
algorithms can be introduced to dynamically adjust the generation resolution and frame rate based on device 
performance. Additionally, for interdisciplinary applications, domain knowledge graphs (such as mathematical 
concept relationships or physical law dependencies) should be constructed to ensure that the GAI-generated 
content aligns strictly with educational objectives, avoiding technological overcomplication that diverges from 
the core of education. Future work will involve collaboration with educational technology experts and subject 
teachers to iteratively refine the technical solutions, driving the transition of GAI from an experimental tool to 
an inclusive educational infrastructure.
